```{r}
         ey = exp(ap$fit), lb = exp(ap$fit - 1.96 * ap$se.fit), ub = exp(ap$fit + 1.96 * ap$se.fit))

ggplot(and, aes(x = aadt, y = ey)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lb, ymax = ub), fill = bu_greyfill, alpha = .4) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_rug(data = cs, aes(x = aadt), inherit.aes = FALSE, sides = "b",
           color = bu_grey, alpha = .6) +
  facet_wrap(~ type, labeller = labeller(type = c("red light" = "Red-light cameras",
                                                  "speed" = "Speed cameras",
                                                  "stop sign" = "Stop-sign cameras"))) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()),
                breaks = c(1000, 10000, 100000)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Average daily traffic (log scale)", y = "Expected tickets per month") +
  theme_bu()
```

Read each panel where its rug is. Every line is drawn across the full range of traffic in the data, but the camera types don't share that range: `r sum(cs$type == "stop sign" & cs$aadt < 10000)` of the `r sum(cs$type == "stop sign")` stop-sign cameras sit on roads with fewer than 10,000 vehicles a day, and only `r sum(cs$type == "stop sign" & cs$aadt > 30000)` on roads busier than 30,000, so the steep right end of that panel — and its wide interval — is the model extending the stop-sign effect onto arterials where DC has very few stop-sign cameras. Red-light cameras are the reverse: none sits on a road with fewer than `r scales::comma(min(cs$aadt[cs$type == "red light"]), 100)` vehicles a day.

@fig-cam-inc is the "neighborhood" story — the income gradient — computed as average predictions: each camera stays at its own type, speed limit, traffic, crashes, and % Black; I set its tract's median income to each value in turn, predict tickets per month for every camera, and average.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"
#| label: fig-cam-inc
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Average expected tickets per month across tract median household income. Every camera held at its observed values on the other variables. 95% delta-method intervals. Ticks along the bottom mark the observed cameras."
#| fig-alt: !expr 'sprintf("Average expected tickets per camera per month plotted against tract median household income from $25,000 to $225,000, with a 95 percent interval. The line falls steadily, from about %d tickets per month at $25,000 to about %d at $225,000. A rug along the bottom shows the cameras: only %d sit in tracts below $40,000, and most are between $60,000 and $150,000.", round(inc_avg$estimate[1]), round(inc_avg$estimate[nrow(inc_avg)]), sum(cs$medinc < 40))'

inc_grid <- seq(25, 225, by = 10)          # $ thousands

inc_avg <- avg_predictions(c_nb, type = "response",
                           newdata = mutate(cs, months = 1),
                           variables = list(lninc = log(inc_grid))) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(medinc = exp(lninc))

ggplot(inc_avg, aes(x = medinc, y = estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = bu_greyfill, alpha = .4) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_rug(data = cs, aes(x = medinc), inherit.aes = FALSE, sides = "b",
           color = bu_grey, alpha = .6) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(suffix = "k")) +
  labs(x = "Tract median household income", y = "Average expected tickets per month") +
  theme_bu()
```

The average camera in a $`r inc_grid[1]`k tract writes `r scales::comma(inc_avg$estimate[1])` tickets a month; the same camera in a $`r inc_grid[length(inc_grid)]`k tract writes `r scales::comma(inc_avg$estimate[nrow(inc_avg)])`. That's a big difference, and it's on top of the road. But notice how wide the interval is — the negative binomial is honest about how much camera-to-camera variation the model doesn't explain — and look at the rug. Only `r sum(cs$medinc < 40)` cameras sit in tracts with median incomes below \$40,000, and `r sum(cs$medinc < 25)` below \$25,000, so the steep left end of the curve is where the model has the least data, and where the interval is widest. The \$50k-to-\$150k comparison below sits where the data are.

As in Part 1, here is what `avg_predictions` does, computed by hand at two incomes: set every camera's tract income to \$50,000, predict tickets per month for every camera (with $d_i = 1$), average; repeat at \$150,000.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"
#| label: tbl-cam-avg-hand
#| tbl-cap: "Average predicted tickets per camera per month, by hand and from marginaleffects."

avg_inc <- function(inc) {
  nd <- mutate(cs, lninc = log(inc), months = 1)
  mean(predict(c_nb, newdata = nd, type = "response"))
}

tibble(`Tract median income` = c("$50,000", "$150,000"),
       `By hand` = c(avg_inc(50), avg_inc(150)),
       marginaleffects = c(avg_predictions(c_nb, newdata = mutate(cs, months = 1), type = "response",
                                           variables = list(lninc = log(c(50, 150))))$estimate)) %>%
  kbl(digits = 1) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

The average-effects version of the \$50k-versus-\$150k comparison, with every camera at its own observed values:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"

# contrast: each camera's prediction at ln(50) minus its prediction at ln(150), averaged
c_cmp <- avg_comparisons(c_nb, newdata = mutate(cs, months = 1),
                         variables = list(lninc = log(c(150, 50))))
c_cmp_hand <- mean(predict(c_nb, newdata = mutate(cs, months = 1, lninc = log(50)), type = "response") -
                   predict(c_nb, newdata = mutate(cs, months = 1, lninc = log(150)), type = "response"))
```

Moving every camera's tract from \$150k to \$50k median income adds an average of `r round(abs(c_cmp_hand))` tickets per camera per month (95% interval `r round(min(abs(c(c_cmp$conf.low, c_cmp$conf.high))))` to `r round(max(abs(c(c_cmp$conf.low, c_cmp$conf.high))))`). Across `r nrow(cs)` cameras and twelve months, that's on the order of `r scales::comma(abs(c_cmp_hand) * nrow(cs) * 12, accuracy = 10000)` tickets a year — the scale of the income gradient, if every camera in the city were moved from a rich tract to a poor one.

## Is the income result fragile?

A few checks on the camera model. The specification is the same throughout; only the sample or the fixed effects change.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"
#| label: tbl-cam-robust

r_speed <- glm.nb(update(cam_f, . ~ . - type), data = filter(cs, type == "speed"),
                  control = glm.control(maxit = 100))
r_near  <- glm.nb(cam_f, data = filter(cs, dist_aadt <= 25), control = glm.control(maxit = 100))
r_full  <- glm.nb(cam_f, data = filter(cs, months == 12), control = glm.control(maxit = 100))
r_ward  <- glm.nb(update(cam_f, . ~ . + ward), data = cs, control = glm.control(maxit = 100))

robust_models <- list("Main" = c_nb, "Speed cameras" = r_speed,
                      "Traffic count within 25 m" = r_near, "Live all 12 months" = r_full,
                      "Ward fixed effects" = r_ward)
robust_alpha <- alpha_rows(robust_models)
attr(robust_alpha, "position") <- c(7, 8)

modelsummary(robust_models,
             stars = TRUE, add_rows = robust_alpha,
             coef_map = c("pctblack" = "% Black", "lninc" = "ln(median income)",
                          "lnaadt" = "ln(daily traffic)"),
             gof_map = c("nobs"),
             title = "Robustness of the camera model. All models include the full set of road covariates.",
             notes = "Negative binomial; offset ln(months live).")
```

The income coefficient holds up among speed cameras alone (`r sprintf("%.3f", coef(r_speed)["lninc"])`), among the `r sum(cs$dist_aadt <= 25)` cameras whose traffic count segment is within 25 m (`r sprintf("%.3f", coef(r_near)["lninc"])`), and among cameras live the full year (`r sprintf("%.3f", coef(r_full)["lninc"])`). It is weakest with ward fixed effects (`r sprintf("%.3f", coef(r_ward)["lninc"])`, $p$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", coef(summary(r_ward))["lninc", 4])`), which use only the variation in income among cameras in the same ward. Wards account for `r round(100 * summary(lm(lninc ~ ward, data = cs))$r.squared)`% of the variance in log income across these cameras, so the fixed effects set aside about half of it. % Black stays near zero throughout; it is never positive and distinguishable from zero. I'd describe the income result as consistent but not overwhelming — which, given $\widehat\alpha$ of about `r round(1 / c_nb$theta, 1)`, is about what we should expect from `r nrow(cs)` cameras.

# Putting the two stages together

Tickets written in a tract are the number of cameras times the tickets each one writes. So which stage drives the difference between Black and white neighborhoods? @tbl-quintiles sorts all `r nrow(tracts)` tracts into fifths by % Black and shows each stage, plus the product, without any model.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"
#| label: tbl-quintiles
#| tbl-cap: "Cameras and tickets by fifth of tracts, sorted by percent Black. Tickets are annualized (a camera's tickets divided by its live months, times 12)."

quint <- tracts %>%
  mutate(fifth = ntile(pctblack, 5)) %>%
  group_by(fifth) %>%
  summarise(Tracts = n(),
            `Mean % Black` = mean(pctblack),
            `Median income ($000)` = median(medinc, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Share with a camera` = mean(ncams > 0),
            `Cameras per tract` = mean(ncams),
            `Tickets per camera per month` = sum(tickets) / sum(ncams) / 12,
            `Tickets per tract per year` = mean(tickets))

quint %>%
  mutate(fifth = c("Least Black", "2", "3", "4", "Most Black")) %>%
  rename(`Fifth of tracts` = fifth) %>%
  kbl(digits = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 2, 2, 0, 0), format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

The answer is placement. The share of tracts with any camera climbs from `r round(100 * quint[[5]][1])`% in the least-Black fifth to `r round(100 * quint[[5]][5])`% in the most-Black fifth, and cameras per tract from `r round(quint[[6]][1], 2)` to `r round(quint[[6]][5], 2)`. Tickets per camera barely move across the fifths — if anything, the least-Black fifth's cameras write the most, which runs opposite to the income gradient in Part 2, since the least-Black tracts are also the richest. That has to come from the roads those cameras sit on, which this table, unlike the model, doesn't hold constant. So the most-Black fifth of tracts absorbs `r round(quint[[8]][5] / quint[[8]][1], 1)` times as many tickets per tract as the least-Black fifth, and almost all of that comes from having more cameras, not from cameras that write more.

That's a descriptive decomposition. Now let's do it properly, in one model.

## A hurdle model for tickets per tract

The outcome is now the number of tickets written in tract $i$ in a year — each camera's tickets divided by its live months, times twelve, summed over the cameras in the tract, and rounded to a whole number. A tract with no camera has zero tickets, and `r sum(round(tr$tickets) == 0)` of the `r nrow(tr)` tracts in the estimation sample have none. A tract with a camera has thousands: the median among tracts with any tickets is `r format(round(median(tr$tickets[tr$tickets > 0])), big.mark = ",")`.

That's two different processes producing one variable. Something decides whether a tract gets any camera at all, and so whether it gets any tickets. Something else decides how many tickets it gets once it has a camera. A Poisson or negative binomial treats the zeros as just the low end of the same distribution that produces the 20,000s, and it can't produce both the pile of zeros and the long right tail. The **hurdle model** splits the outcome at zero: a binary model for whether the tract clears the hurdle, and a count model, truncated at zero, for how many tickets it gets given that it has.

### The likelihood

Same recipe as before.

**The PMF.** Let $\pi_i$ be the probability tract $i$ clears the hurdle (has any tickets), and let $f_{NB}(y_i \mid \lambda_i, \alpha)$ be the negative binomial PMF from Part 2. Then

$$
f(y_i \mid \pi_i, \lambda_i, \alpha) =
\begin{cases}
1 - \pi_i & \text{if } y_i = 0 \\[8pt]
\pi_i \, \dfrac{f_{NB}(y_i \mid \lambda_i, \alpha)}{1 - f_{NB}(0 \mid \lambda_i, \alpha)} & \text{if } y_i > 0
\end{cases}
$$

The first line is the probability of a zero. The second is the probability of clearing the hurdle times the probability of $y_i$ tickets *given* that the count is positive. That's why the negative binomial is divided by $1 - f_{NB}(0)$: the count part only describes $y = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$, and dividing by the probability of being positive makes those probabilities sum to one. This is a **zero-truncated** negative binomial. From Part 1, the negative binomial probability of a zero is

$$
f_{NB}(0 \mid \lambda_i, \alpha) = \left(\frac{\alpha^{-1}}{\alpha^{-1} + \lambda_i}\right)^{\alpha^{-1}} = (1 + \alpha\lambda_i)^{-1/\alpha}
$$

**The joint probability.** Assuming the tracts are independent, the zeros contribute $1 - \pi_i$ and the positives contribute the second line:

$$
L(\pi, \lambda, \alpha \mid y) = \prod_{y_i = 0} (1 - \pi_i) \prod_{y_i > 0} \pi_i \, \frac{f_{NB}(y_i \mid \lambda_i, \alpha)}{1 - (1 + \alpha\lambda_i)^{-1/\alpha}}
$$

**Take logs.** Write $I_i = 1$ if $y_i > 0$ and $I_i = 0$ otherwise. The log of the product is

$$
\ln L(\pi, \lambda, \alpha \mid y) = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big[ (1 - I_i)\ln(1 - \pi_i) + I_i \ln \pi_i \Big]}_{\text{the hurdle}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n} I_i \Big[ \ln f_{NB}(y_i \mid \lambda_i, \alpha) - \ln\big(1 - (1 + \alpha\lambda_i)^{-1/\alpha}\big) \Big]}_{\text{the count, given } y_i > 0}
$$

Look at the first sum. It is exactly the binary log-likelihood from [the likelihood notes](likelihood26.html) — the ones and the zeros, mirror images, with $I_i$ doing the switching — where the "ones" are tracts with any tickets. The second sum is the negative binomial log-likelihood from Part 2, over the positive tracts only, minus the log of the truncation term. $\ln f_{NB}$ is the expression we derived there:

$$
\ln f_{NB}(y_i \mid \lambda_i, \alpha) = \ln\Gamma(y_i + \alpha^{-1}) - \ln\Gamma(\alpha^{-1}) - \ln(y_i!) + y_i\ln\alpha + y_i\ln\lambda_i - (y_i + \alpha^{-1})\ln(1 + \alpha\lambda_i)
$$

**Parameterize.** Each part gets its own link and its own coefficients. The hurdle is a logit, and the count is log-linear:

$$
\pi_i = \Lambda(z_i\gamma) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z_i\gamma}}, \qquad \lambda_i = e^{x_i\beta}
$$

$z_i$ and $x_i$ can be different variables; here they are the same four (% Black, crashes, major road, income), so we can compare how each one works in each part.

**Separability.** Here is the convenient thing. $\gamma$ appears only in the first sum, and $\beta$ and $\alpha$ appear only in the second. So maximizing the whole log-likelihood is the same as maximizing each sum on its own: a logit of $I_i$ on $z_i$ across all tracts, and a zero-truncated negative binomial of $y_i$ on $x_i$ across the tracts with $y_i > 0$. The hurdle model's log-likelihood is the sum of the two.

**The gradient for the count part.** The truncation term adds a piece to each of the negative binomial scores from Part 2. Writing $f_{0i} = (1 + \alpha\lambda_i)^{-1/\alpha}$, the derivative of $-\ln(1 - f_{0i})$ with respect to $\beta$ is $-\frac{f_{0i}}{1 - f_{0i}}\frac{\lambda_i}{1 + \alpha\lambda_i}x_i'$, so

$$
\frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \beta} = \sum_{y_i > 0} \left[ \frac{y_i - \lambda_i}{1 + \alpha\lambda_i} - \frac{f_{0i}}{1 - f_{0i}}\,\frac{\lambda_i}{1 + \alpha\lambda_i} \right] x_i'
$$

and the score for $\alpha$ is the negative binomial's plus $\frac{f_{0i}}{1 - f_{0i}}\left[\alpha^{-2}\ln(1 + \alpha\lambda_i) - \frac{\lambda_i}{\alpha(1 + \alpha\lambda_i)}\right]$ for each positive tract.

### Estimation

`pscl::hurdle()` fits this model, but `pscl` isn't in the course library, and since the two parts separate, we don't need it: `glm` for the hurdle, and our own optimizer for the truncated count.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"
#| label: tbl-hurdle
#| tbl-cap: "Hurdle model of tickets per tract per year. Left: logit for any tickets (all tracts). Right: zero-truncated negative binomial for the number of tickets (tracts with any)."

trh <- tr %>% mutate(y = round(tickets), any = as.integer(y > 0))

# the hurdle: logit of any tickets, all tracts
h_bin <- glm(any ~ pctblack + lncrashes + lnmajorkm + lninc, data = trh, family = binomial)

# the count: zero-truncated NB, tracts with any tickets
pos <- filter(trh, y > 0)
Zc <- model.matrix(~ pctblack + lncrashes + lnmajorkm + lninc, pos)
yc <- pos$y
kc <- ncol(Zc)

# log-likelihood; par = (beta_1, ..., beta_k, ln alpha)
tnb_ll <- function(par) {
  b <- par[1:kc]
  a <- exp(par[kc + 1])
  lambda <- as.vector(exp(Zc %*% b))
  f0 <- (1 + a * lambda)^(-1 / a)
  sum(lgamma(yc + 1 / a) - lgamma(1 / a) - lgamma(yc + 1) + yc * log(a) + yc * log(lambda) -
        (yc + 1 / a) * log(1 + a * lambda) - log(1 - f0))
}

# gradient: NB scores plus the truncation pieces; last element is for ln alpha
tnb_gr <- function(par) {
  b <- par[1:kc]
  a <- exp(par[kc + 1])
  lambda <- as.vector(exp(Zc %*% b))
  f0 <- (1 + a * lambda)^(-1 / a)
  g_b <- colSums(Zc * ((yc - lambda) / (1 + a * lambda) -
                         f0 / (1 - f0) * lambda / (1 + a * lambda)))
  g_a_nb <- sum(-a^-2 * (digamma(yc + 1 / a) - digamma(1 / a) - log(1 + a * lambda)) +
                  (yc - lambda) / (a * (1 + a * lambda)))
  g_a_tr <- sum(f0 / (1 - f0) * (a^-2 * log(1 + a * lambda) - lambda / (a * (1 + a * lambda))))
  c(g_b, a * (g_a_nb + g_a_tr))
}

# start from an untruncated NB on the positive tracts
nb_start <- glm.nb(y ~ pctblack + lncrashes + lnmajorkm + lninc, data = pos)
h_cnt <- optim(c(coef(nb_start), log(1 / nb_start$theta)), tnb_ll, tnb_gr, method = "BFGS",
               control = list(fnscale = -1, maxit = 10000, reltol = 1e-14))
H_cnt <- optimHess(h_cnt$par, tnb_ll, tnb_gr)
V_cnt <- solve(-H_cnt)
se_cnt <- sqrt(diag(V_cnt))

h_alpha <- exp(h_cnt$par[kc + 1])
h_alpha_se <- h_alpha * se_cnt[kc + 1]
h_ll <- as.numeric(logLik(h_bin)) + h_cnt$value

stars <- function(z) case_when(abs(z) > 3.29 ~ "***", abs(z) > 2.58 ~ "**",
                               abs(z) > 1.96 ~ "*", abs(z) > 1.645 ~ "+", TRUE ~ "")
cell <- function(b, se) sprintf("%.3f%s (%.3f)", b, stars(b / se), se)

tibble(Variable = c(tract_labels[names(coef(h_bin))[-1]], "Constant", "alpha"),
       `Hurdle: any tickets (logit)` = c(cell(coef(h_bin), sqrt(diag(vcov(h_bin))))[c(2:5, 1)], ""),
       `Count: tickets, given any (truncated NB)` = c(cell(h_cnt$par[1:kc], se_cnt[1:kc])[c(2:5, 1)],
                                                     sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", h_alpha, h_alpha_se))) %>%
  bind_rows(tibble(Variable = c("Num.Obs.", "Log.Lik."),
                   `Hurdle: any tickets (logit)` = c(as.character(nobs(h_bin)),
                                                     sprintf("%.3f", logLik(h_bin))),
                   `Count: tickets, given any (truncated NB)` = c(as.character(nrow(pos)),
                                                                  sprintf("%.3f", h_cnt$value)))) %>%
  kbl(align = "lcc") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>%
  footnote(general = "Standard errors in parentheses. + p < 0.1, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001. alpha's standard error by the delta method from ln alpha; no stars, since alpha = 0 is on the boundary (use the likelihood ratio test).")
```

The hurdle model's log-likelihood is the sum of the two parts: `r sprintf("%.3f", logLik(h_bin))` + (`r sprintf("%.3f", h_cnt$value)`) = `r sprintf("%.3f", h_ll)`.

Read the two columns side by side, because that's the point of the model.

**The hurdle.** Whether a tract has any camera — and so any tickets — depends on crashes, road, and race. Each ten points of % Black multiplies the odds of having a camera by `r round(exp(10 * coef(h_bin)["pctblack"]), 2)` ($z$ = `r round(coef(summary(h_bin))["pctblack", 3], 2)`), holding crashes, road, and income constant. Income does nothing here (`r sprintf("%.3f", coef(h_bin)["lninc"])`, $z$ = `r round(coef(summary(h_bin))["lninc", 3], 2)`).

**The count.** Among tracts that have a camera, more road means more tickets — more road means room for more cameras — and % Black still points up (`r sprintf("%.4f", h_cnt$par[2])`, $z$ = `r round(h_cnt$par[2] / se_cnt[2], 2)`), less precisely. That coefficient mixes two things: tracts with more Black residents that have *a* camera tend to have *more* cameras (the intensive side of placement), while, from Part 2, cameras in poorer tracts write more tickets each. Income's coefficient (`r sprintf("%.3f", h_cnt$par[5])`, $z$ = `r round(h_cnt$par[5] / se_cnt[5], 2)`) is negative here, as it was for yield, but imprecise. The hurdle model splits the outcome at zero; it can't, by itself, separate the number of cameras from the tickets each one writes. That's what the camera-level model in Part 2 is for.

**The truncation.** $\widehat\alpha$ = `r round(h_alpha, 3)`. With counts in the thousands, the negative binomial probability of a zero is tiny — the largest $f_{NB}(0 \mid \widehat\lambda_i, \widehat\alpha)$ among the positive tracts is `r format(signif(max((1 + h_alpha * exp(Zc %*% h_cnt$par[1:kc]))^(-1 / h_alpha)), 2), scientific = TRUE)` — so dividing by $1 - f_{NB}(0)$ changes almost nothing, and the truncated estimates are essentially those of an ordinary negative binomial on the positive tracts (log-likelihood `r sprintf("%.3f", logLik(nb_start))` against `r sprintf("%.3f", h_cnt$value)`). That won't be true with small counts, where the truncation term does real work.

### Putting it back together: expected tickets

The hurdle model's expected count combines the two parts. The probability of clearing the hurdle times the expected count given that it's cleared:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[y_i \mid z_i, x_i] &= Pr(y_i > 0) \times E[y_i \mid y_i > 0] \\[6pt]
&= \pi_i \times \frac{\lambda_i}{1 - (1 + \alpha\lambda_i)^{-1/\alpha}}
\end{aligned}
$$

The second factor is the mean of a zero-truncated negative binomial: the untruncated mean, $\lambda_i$, scaled up by one over the probability of being positive. Because the expected count is a product, its log is a sum, $\ln E[y_i] = \ln \pi_i + \ln E[y_i \mid y_i > 0]$, and the difference between two tracts splits exactly into a hurdle part and a count part.

For uncertainty, I simulate. The two parts are estimated separately, so their estimates are independent: draw 1,000 $\widetilde\gamma$ from $MVN(\widehat\gamma, \widehat V_\gamma)$ and 1,000 $(\widetilde\beta, \widetilde{\ln\alpha})$ from $MVN$ with the inverse negative Hessian of the count part, compute all three quantities for each draw, and take percentiles.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"
#| label: fig-hurdle
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Hurdle model quantities across percent Black: the probability a tract has any tickets, expected tickets given any, and expected tickets overall. Crashes, road, and income at their medians. 95% simulation intervals. Ticks along the bottom mark the observed tracts."
#| fig-alt: !expr 'sprintf("Three panels against percent Black from 0 to 100, each with a 95 percent interval and a rug of observed tracts along the bottom. Left, the probability a tract has any tickets rises from %.2f to %.2f. Middle, expected tickets per year given any rises from about %s to %s, with a wide interval. Right, expected tickets per tract per year rises from about %s to %s.", hq$pi[1], hq$pi[101], scales::comma(hq$cond[1], 100), scales::comma(hq$cond[101], 100), scales::comma(hq$ey[1], 100), scales::comma(hq$ey[101], 100))'

Xh <- model.matrix(~ pctblack + lncrashes + lnmajorkm + lninc,
                   tibble(pctblack = 0:100,
                          lncrashes = median(trh$lncrashes),
                          lnmajorkm = median(trh$lnmajorkm),
                          lninc = median(trh$lninc)))

# the three quantities at a given gamma, beta, alpha
hurdle_q <- function(g, b, a) {
  pi <- plogis(as.vector(Xh %*% g))
  lambda <- as.vector(exp(Xh %*% b))
  cond <- lambda / (1 - (1 + a * lambda)^(-1 / a))
  tibble(pctblack = 0:100, pi = pi, cond = cond, ey = pi * cond)
}

hq <- hurdle_q(coef(h_bin), h_cnt$par[1:kc], h_alpha)

g_sim <- mvrnorm(1000, coef(h_bin), vcov(h_bin))
c_sim <- mvrnorm(1000, h_cnt$par, V_cnt)
hq_sim <- map_dfr(1:1000, ~ hurdle_q(g_sim[.x, ], c_sim[.x, 1:kc], exp(c_sim[.x, kc + 1])),
                  .id = "draw")

hq_long <- hq_sim %>%
  pivot_longer(c(pi, cond, ey), names_to = "quantity") %>%
  group_by(pctblack, quantity) %>%
  summarise(lb = quantile(value, .025), ub = quantile(value, .975), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(pivot_longer(hq, c(pi, cond, ey), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "est"),
            by = c("pctblack", "quantity")) %>%
  mutate(quantity = factor(quantity, levels = c("pi", "cond", "ey"),
                           labels = c("Pr(any tickets)", "E[tickets | any]", "E[tickets]")))

ggplot(hq_long, aes(x = pctblack, y = est)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lb, ymax = ub), fill = bu_greyfill, alpha = .4) +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_rug(data = trh, aes(x = pctblack), inherit.aes = FALSE, sides = "b",
           color = bu_grey, alpha = .6) +
  facet_wrap(~ quantity, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(accuracy = .01, drop0trailing = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "% Black", y = NULL) +
  theme_bu()
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"
#| label: tbl-hurdle-decomp
#| tbl-cap: "Expected tickets per tract per year from the hurdle model, at 10% and 90% Black (other variables at their medians), and how the difference divides between the two parts."

h_10 <- filter(hq, pctblack == 10)
h_90 <- filter(hq, pctblack == 90)
ey_diff_sim <- hq_sim %>%
  filter(pctblack %in% c(10, 90)) %>%
  select(draw, pctblack, ey) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = pctblack, values_from = ey, names_prefix = "b") %>%
  mutate(diff = b90 - b10)

log_ratio <- c(pi = log(h_90$pi / h_10$pi), cond = log(h_90$cond / h_10$cond))

tibble(Quantity = c("Pr(any tickets)", "E[tickets | any]", "E[tickets]"),
       `10% Black` = c(h_10$pi, h_10$cond, h_10$ey),
       `90% Black` = c(h_90$pi, h_90$cond, h_90$ey),
       `Ratio, 90 / 10` = c(h_90$pi / h_10$pi, h_90$cond / h_10$cond, h_90$ey / h_10$ey),
       `Share of the log ratio` = c(log_ratio / sum(log_ratio), 1)) %>%
  kbl(digits = c(0, 2, 2, 2, 2), format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

A tract with median crashes, road, and income that is 10% Black is expected to have `r scales::comma(h_10$ey, 1)` tickets a year; the same tract 90% Black, `r scales::comma(h_90$ey, 1)` — `r round(h_90$ey / h_10$ey, 1)` times as many, a difference of `r scales::comma(h_90$ey - h_10$ey, 1)` (95% simulation interval `r scales::comma(quantile(ey_diff_sim$diff, .025), 1)` to `r scales::comma(quantile(ey_diff_sim$diff, .975), 1)`). The decomposition says where it comes from. The 90% Black tract is `r round(h_90$pi / h_10$pi, 2)` times as likely to have any camera, and, given that it has one, expects `r round(h_90$cond / h_10$cond, 2)` times as many tickets. On the log scale, `r round(100 * log_ratio["pi"] / sum(log_ratio))`% of the gap is the hurdle — whether the tract has a camera at all — and `r round(100 * log_ratio["cond"] / sum(log_ratio))`% is the count, which from the descriptive table and Part 2 is mostly the number of cameras rather than tickets per camera.

So the model and the descriptive table agree: the difference in enforcement between Black and white neighborhoods in DC is a placement story, at both the extensive margin (whether a tract has a camera) and the intensive one (how many it has). The rug is a reminder of where to believe it. The 10% and 90% comparisons sit where the tracts are; the middle of each curve rests on the few mixed tracts DC has.

# What this does and doesn't show

Putting these together, the evidence says DC's cameras are more densely placed in Black neighborhoods than crashes, road length, and income can account for, and that once a camera is placed, it writes more tickets in poorer neighborhoods than its road and traffic can account for. The hurdle model puts the two together and says the first of these dominates: most of the difference in tickets per tract between Black and white neighborhoods comes from whether, and how many, cameras are there. The placement result replicates @farrell2018dcpc with newer data and more controls.

There are several things it does not show:

- **Who gets the tickets.** Tract demographics describe the residents of the tract where a camera stands, not the drivers it tickets. The twelve cameras on Southern Avenue and Eastern Avenue sit on the Maryland line, and many of the drivers they ticket presumably live in Maryland. DDOT does not publish ticket-level driver residence, so "enforcement lands in Black neighborhoods" is a claim about where cameras are, not about who pays.
- **Intent.** The placement model is conditional on crashes and roads, but DDOT also places cameras in response to resident complaints, school zones, and pedestrian deaths that a four-year crash count may not capture. An omitted "need" variable correlated with % Black would bias the race coefficient up.
- **Danger.** A camera that writes a lot of tickets is a camera where a lot of people speed. The yield result might mean drivers in poorer neighborhoods speed more on comparable roads — which could be because those roads are designed for speed in ways AADT and the speed limit don't measure. Cameras might be doing exactly the job they were placed to do.
- **Novelty.** Drivers learn where cameras are. The offset handles the number of months a camera was live, but not where those months fall in the camera's life, and that matters — see @fig-novelty below.

DDOT's monthly counts go back to September 2022, so we can look at what happens to a camera's tickets after it is switched on. @fig-novelty takes every camera whose first live month came after January 2023 and that has at least 18 live months, divides each month's tickets by that camera's average over its months 13 through 18, and plots the median ratio by month since the camera went live.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"
#| label: fig-novelty
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "Tickets in each month since a camera went live, relative to the same camera's average in months 13-18. Median across cameras first live after January 2023 with at least 18 live months."
#| fig-alt: !expr 'sprintf("Median ratio of monthly tickets to the camera average in months 13 to 18, plotted for months 1 through 18 after a camera goes live, across %d cameras. Month 1 is low, at %.2f, because it is usually a partial month. Month 2 is the peak, at %.2f. The ratio then falls steadily, reaching about 1 by month %d and staying there.", n_distinct(nov$id), nov_curve$ratio[1], nov_curve$ratio[2], min(nov_curve$k[nov_curve$k > 2 & nov_curve$ratio <= 1.06]))'

monthly <- read_csv(here::here("data", "dccameras-monthly.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# months since the camera's first live month, counting that month as 1
nov <- monthly %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(first = min(month),
         k = 12 * (as.numeric(format(month, "%Y")) - as.numeric(format(first, "%Y"))) +
             as.numeric(format(month, "%m")) - as.numeric(format(first, "%m")) + 1,
         nlive = n()) %>%
  filter(first > as.Date("2023-01-01"), nlive >= 18) %>%
  mutate(ratio = tickets / mean(tickets[k %in% 13:18])) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(k <= 18)

nov_curve <- nov %>% group_by(k) %>% summarise(ratio = median(ratio), n = n())

ggplot(nov_curve, aes(x = k, y = ratio)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, color = bu_grey, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = bu_green, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = bu_green, size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:18) +
  labs(x = "Month since the camera went live",
       y = "Tickets relative to months 13-18") +
  theme_bu()
```

The first month is usually partial, so ignore it. In its second month, the median camera writes `r round(nov_curve$ratio[2], 1)` times as many tickets as it will in its second year, and the excess fades over the rest of the first year. For the cross-section, that means a camera installed in 2026 is observed in its high-ticket phase, while one installed in 2023 is observed at its steady state. If newer cameras are disproportionately in some kinds of neighborhoods, the yield model will pick that up as a neighborhood effect. Restricting to cameras live all twelve months (the robustness table) removes the very newest cameras and leaves the income coefficient where it was, which is reassuring but not a fix. The fix is to model the panel — camera-months, with time since installation in the model — rather than the cross-section.
